messages.subject: Genetic map construction in nested association mapping population
messages.subject_clean: Genetic map construction in nested association mapping population
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,
is it possible to construct a genetic map of a NAM double haploid population? I have 21 families sharing one common parent. Per family there are 50 offsprings. Is it better to calculate genetic map for each family separatly, even there are just 50 genotypes, or calculate over whole population(1050 genotypes, but weird allele frequencies(I guess)).

Thanks a lot for your suggestions.

Sincerely Tobias

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map construction in nested association mapping population
messages.subject_clean: [Rqtl-disc] Genetic map construction in nested association mapping population
messages.body_plain:
I think you should be able to pool them to estimate a common map, but I would also look at the family-specific maps, to see if there are any regions with big differences in recombination rates.

I would code each as A:B where A is the common parent and B is the other parent. In a particular family, if a marker is not segregating, I'd give all offspring missing genotypes.

karl

messages.subject: Does read.cross automatically initiate estimation of genetic map if no chr/pos data are provided?
messages.subject_clean: Does read.cross automatically initiate estimation of genetic map if no chr/pos data are provided?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Karl,

I try to load a large dataset (131 RILs, around 133k markers). I have no genetic map yet. I just want to generate a "cross" object to test it with the new R package ASMap (http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ASMap/ASMap.pdf). This is a new package which uses "cross" objects and the algorithm from MSTmap for high-density genetic mapping.

However, if I try to load data like this:

# load data
geno <- read.cross(format=c("csvr"), dir="D:/Mydata", "mydata.csv", na.strings=c("-","NA"), genotypes=c("A","H","B","D","C"), alleles=c("A","B"))

or

# load data
geno <- read.cross(format=c("csvr"), dir="D:/Mydata", "mydata.csv")

I get in both cases:

--Read the following data:
	 131  individuals
	 132862  markers
	 1  phenotypes
 --Estimating genetic map

 And then it will take forever (or run out of memory).

Can I somehow avoid the step with estimation of the genetic map? I just need to generate the cross object.

Best regards,
Eva

messages.subject: Error in names(typingsX) <- temp
messages.body_plain:
I have two files that were output by RQTL using write.cross in 2013. (I have many, but the point is there is a group that will load and a group that will not). They are subsets of the same data, and the only difference is total number of markers and individuals.  One group, which has more individuals and fewer markers, loads fine with this command:

x<-read.cross(format="csv", file="file.csv", na.strings=c("-"), genotypes=c("AA", "AB", "BB"), convertXdata=TRUE)

The other does not, and throws this error.

Error in names(typingsX) <- temp :

  'names' attribute [2] must be the same length as the vector [1]

They are subsets of the same data, and I have examined them multiple times for differences like stray commas or extra columns. I've had all of those kinds of problems before though, and they usually throw different and more interpretable errors. The format of the marker names and individual names are the same.

>From what I can tell there has not been a change in acceptable input data since 2013, and since these were output by RQTL I cannot figure out what the problem is. I see that a similar error has been posted before, but no solution was posted.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] "Didn't converge" warning.
messages.body_plain:
Estimation of the genetic map uses an iterative algorithm; the warning message says that the map estimates didn't converge to the final estimates yet.

You'll want to use est.map to get a final map, and then replace.map to plug it into the cross object.

karl

messages.subject: binary scantwo using too much memory
messages.subject_clean: binary scantwo using too much memory
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I was wondering if anyone else has run into problems running scantwo permutations using a binary model. I can run normal traits in about 6 hours on my cluster but a binary model in the same dataset times out after 24 hours using the same cluster configuration.

Here are the details:
I have a 4way cross with 400 individuals genotyped at 1200 markers. I have already run scantwo perms and used a stepwise model to find qtl for 12 'normal' traits using 'hk'. However, I also have a 2part trait that I would like to investigate. Thus far I have run scanone '2part' and found there is at least one qtl. In order to run scantwo I split my trait up into two traits, one is binary and the other is normal with the spike of extreme values removed. The normal model runs similar to my previous traits but the binary takes forever and I'm not sure if it is just getting stuck or actually running.

# Splitting up 2part phenotype :
rust.bi <http://rust.bi> <- as.numeric(pull.pheno(data, 5) > .9)
data$pheno <- cbind(data$pheno, rust.bi <http://rust.bi>=rust.bi <http://rust.bi>)
rust.norm <- as.numeric(pull.pheno(data, 5))
rust.norm <- as.numeric(sub(1.00000000, NA, rust.norm))
data$pheno <- cbind(data$pheno, rust.norm=rust.norm)

# scantwo perms
perms.out<-scantwo(data, pheno.col="rust.bi <http://rust.bi>" , model="binary", method="hk",n.perm=1000, n.cluster=24, addcovar=cov_cross, perm.strata=cov_cross)

Any ideas about how to move beyond scanone with a 2part traits?

Thanks,
Liz Milano

messages.subject: Identifying two close QTL
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I was wondering if it is possible to disentangle two very close potential QTL. My problem is, using another program, I got a QTL with two distinct significant peaks, with a trough between which was non-significant. There are several markers in the area. Under each of the peaks I find a good candidate gene for the phenotype, so I want to find out if it is possible to say with confidence that the QTL are separate.

The method I have used so far in R/qtl is to do a single QTL scan, which gave me a QTL on chromosome 1 @ 108cM, with a LOD score of 4.72. I then used makeqtl for two QTL at 96cM and 115cM (the positions of the two peaks) which gave me a LOD score of 5.67. The drop argument in the summary suggested the QTL at 96cM was significant (p < 0.05) whereas the QTL at 115cM was only suggestive (p < 0.1). Does the increased LOD with the two QTL model suggest there really are two QTL? Is there a better way to do this, or is it not possible?

Thank you in advance for your replies,

David

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Identifying two close QTL
messages.body_plain:
I would look at the 2d scan on that chromosome (with scantwo); pretty much the same as what you did, but also varying the locations of the two loci.

I would ignore the p-value in the "drop one qtl at a time" table, as this is pointwise - doesn't adjust for the genome scan.

The two-QTL model will give a bigger LOD score than the best single-QTL model; the key question is, how much bigger does it need to be for you to conclude that there's good evidence for a second QTL? I use the threshold from a permutation test in the single-QTL scan, and would consider 5.67 - 4.72 = 0.95 to be quite weak.

karl

messages.subject: 1000 permutation vs multple traits/phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

With the multiple traits/phenotypes - do I need to run separate analysis for each trait using 1000 permutations each time; or I can just run the 1000 permutations ONCE and then use "pheno.col=xx" to analyze the traits one by one? Note: I'm using scantwo and the multiple imputation method.

Thank you for your time; and Happy Holidays.
messages.body_snippet:
Hi:

With the multiple traits/phenotypes - do I need to run separate analysis for each trait using 1000 permutations each time; or I can just run the 1000 permutations ONCE and then use "pheno.col=xx"

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] 1000 permutation vs multple traits/phenotypes
messages.body_plain:
If the phenotypes all have the same distribution, the permutation thresholds will be the same, and so you could just use any one phenotype to derive permutations.

But if there are important differences in the phenotypes' marginal distributions, there can be important differences in the significance thresholds, and so it would be safest to derive separate thresholds for each trait.

One trick that I've used in the case of gene expression phenotypes (where we had 25k genes x 6 tissues of phenotypes) was to convert each trait to normal quantiles, in which case you've forced them all to have the same marginal distribution and so you can just use permutations from a single phenotype and apply the results to all traits.

karl

Dear Karl,

I am trying to figure out what the intercept is in the results of fitqtl for a four-way cross. Here is an example of what I get as an output:

 Intercept 1...@82.0.BC 1...@82.0.AD 1...@82.0.BD
 -62.56465  254.87756   79.25001  242.06471

At first, I thought it was the mean value across all individuals, but it is clearly not that. Is it instead the mean value for the AC genotype?

Thanks a ton,

David

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Intercept for four-way cross
messages.body_plain:
The intercept from fitqtl, for a 4-way cross, would be the average for individuals that have genotype AC at all QTL.

regards,
karl
